Article content: {"cover_media":"3_2072679446260387840","entities":{"urls":[{"text":"https://www.glean.com/blog/introducing-independent-agents"}]},"media_entities":["13_2072591012212649984","3_2072591271374532608"],"plain_text":"Anthropic launched Claude Tag and Andrej Karpathy called it "the 3rd major redesign of LLM UIUX."
The first was web-based chatbots. The second was standalone applications. The third, in his words, is AI that is "significantly more inline with all the other human activity org-wide."
That framing is worth sitting with.
Anthropic's own product team is already running an internal version. 65% of their code is now written by it. The same pattern has spread across engineering, product metrics, support tickets, and incident investigation.
The reason people are paying attention isn't the Slack integration. It's the architectural decision underneath it: one Claude per channel, shared across the entire team. Not one per user. One per channel.
Anyone can see what it's working on. Anyone can pick up where the last person left off. The AI isn't a private tool anymore. It's a participant the whole team steers together.
This is what the shift from AI tools to AI coworkers actually looks like.
But Claude Tag is one layer of what that actually requires. Here's the full picture.
What Changes When AI Goes Multiplayer
Most AI integrations before Claude Tag worked the same way. You open a chat, get a response, close the tab. The next person starts from scratch. No shared state, no continuity, no handoff.
Claude Tag changed one thing architecturally: the agent instance lives at the channel level, not the user level. Everyone in that channel interacts with the same Claude. It builds context from the channel over time, remembers what happened earlier, follows up on threads that have gone quiet.
That single design decision is what Karpathy is pointing to. Once AI operates at the organizational level rather than the individual level, the interaction model changes entirely.
But channel-level is still just one slice of where an organization's knowledge actually lives.
The Context Layer
When an agent needs to act across a real organization, the context that matters is spread across Jira tickets, Confluence docs, GitHub history, and Slack threads from three weeks ago.
An agent working only from the channel where the alert fired is missing most of what it needs.
This is the harder architectural problem. Not just making agents multiplayer, but giving them access to organizational knowledge across every system, permission-aware, always current.
Independent Agents
This is the problem Glean set out to solve.
Enterprises want agents that act autonomously alongside their teams. But letting agents act independently across critical systems introduces real risk if there's no structure around what they can access, what they remember, and what they're allowed to do.
Glean's independent agents are grounded in your company's context, processes, permissions, and connected applications. The agent understands the work, investigates issues, and takes the next best step, while everything it does stays traceable and within the guardrails your organization sets.
Four characteristics make this work in practice.
Identity
Most agents today run as an extension of whoever is using them. They inherit the user's permissions, the user's session, the user's context window.
Independent agents have their own identity. Their own provisioned access to the tools and data they need. Their own presence across the systems they work in.
You can control exactly what each agent can and cannot access. A different agent for engineering than for sales. Different memory, different tools, different data access. Nothing bleeds across.
Every action is traceable back to which agent, with which permissions, took which action, at what time, triggered by what input. That audit trail is what makes autonomous execution actually trustworthy.
Memory
Channel-level memory is powerful. The agent knows what happened in that Slack channel.
Production agents need memory that goes deeper and compounds over time.
They start by learning from the organization's existing knowledge: SOPs, runbooks, documented processes. Before the first incident fires, the agent already knows how the team handles escalations.
Then they learn from every interaction. A mistake made once gets corrected and locked. A pattern that works gets reinforced. Over months, the agent carries institutional knowledge that would take a new hire a year to absorb.
Proactivity
Claude Tag has an ambient mode. It flags relevant information from across the channels it's in without being asked. It follows up on threads that have gone quiet. It surfaces things before you realize you need them.
Most agent setups don't work this way. You ask, it responds. The moment you stop prompting, it stops working.
Production agents need to operate differently. The agent monitors what's happening, identifies what needs attention, and acts without waiting to be asked.
Accountability
The more autonomously an agent operates, the more important it is to see exactly what it did.
Every tool call visible. Every decision explainable. Every action traceable back to the input that triggered it.
And when something goes wrong, there needs to be an immediate off switch. Not a support ticket. Not a config change. An emergency stop that disables the agent everywhere, immediately.
Accountability isn't something you add later. It's what separates an agent you can actually deploy from one you're afraid to run unsupervised.
What This Looks Like in Practice
The clearest example is Glean's OnCall Assistant.
An alert fires. The on-call engineer opens PagerDuty, starts reading logs, searches Confluence for the runbook, checks GitHub for recent deploys, scrolls through Slack to find the last time this happened.
The OnCall Assistant does all of that simultaneously. It reads the escalation, pulls context from Jira, Confluence, GitHub, and recent Slack threads, pursues multiple root-cause theories, drafts a fix, and tags the right owner.
By the time the engineer opens their laptop, the investigation is already done.
 
The agent has its own identity with provisioned access. It learned from the team's runbooks before the first incident ever fired. Every action is fully traceable, with an emergency stop available to admins at any time.
Glean indexes knowledge across an organization's entire stack across 100+ connectors, building a knowledge graph that understands relationships between documents, people, projects, and decisions. The agent doesn't just know a document exists. It knows how it connects to the team that owns it, the project it belongs to, and the decisions that shaped it.
 
The Shift
Karpathy called Claude Tag the third major redesign of how we interact with LLMs.
The shift isn't about a better interface. It's about where the AI lives inside an organization and how it operates within it.
Channel-level context is where this starts. Organizational context across every system is where it goes.
Identity, memory, proactivity, accountability, and a context layer that spans the entire organization. That's what it actually takes to build agents that work like coworkers.
Read more about Glean's independent agents here: https://www.glean.com/blog/introducing-independent-agents
